report.source_text: A 2-day-old Caucasian female patient has been transferred straight from maternity to our hospital. The main concern was reverse peristalsis, together with significant abdominal distention and inability of passing stools with fever. On the same day, an adequate stimulation resulted in defecation, reverse peristalsis stopped, and abdominal distention (circumference) was reduced. Enteral feeding resumed; however, the patient could not pass stools without stimulation.

report.source_text: Within 2 days of the first contrast enema, which was performed on day 4, the patient experienced the start of a high fever. There was no family history of Hirschsprung’s disease mentioned, nor other genetic conditions present suggesting it. Before initiating contrast enema, a rectal examination was done, and no explosive gas and/or fluid release was detected; no feces were in the rectum either. Later on, the status started to deteriorate, and fever became more aggressive, heart and respiratory rate increased, and livedo reticularis started to predominate together with significant abdominal distention, which as time passed, did not reduce with defecation. A digital rectal examination became positive for the explosive release of gas after 3 weeks of hospitalization at our hospital.

report.source_text: While ileostomy was being performed, no transition zone was visualized. After surgical intervention, within 14 days, fever completely abated, and over 4 weeks significant weight gain (2 kg) was observed, both of which were a clear indications of clinical improvement.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 2-day-old Caucasian female presented with reverse peristalsis, significant abdominal distention, inability to pass stools, and fever. Initial stimulation provided temporary relief, but the inability to pass stools without stimulation persisted. A contrast enema on day 4 did not show a transition zone. A first rectal biopsy on day 10 was inconclusive. The patient's condition deteriorated with high fever, increased heart/respiratory rate, livedo reticularis, and worsening abdominal distention. A digital rectal examination became positive for explosive gas release after 3 weeks. On day 75, a surgical intervention (enterostomy) was performed. During this procedure, full-thickness rectal and colonic biopsies were taken, and pathologic examination confirmed total colonic aganglionosis. No transition zone was visualized during the ileostomy. Post-operatively, fever abated within 14 days, and significant weight gain was observed over 4 weeks, indicating clinical improvement.
